title: 3-Read Friday #61: Choral Response, Learning From Mistakes, and Pre-Teaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #61 of 3-Read Friday points readers to three pieces on classroom questioning and intervention design. Pritesh Raichura's 'Choral Response and I Say You Say' unpacks two whole-class oral-response techniques used to sustain attention and participation during explanations, distinguishing low-accountability choral techniques from higher-accountability individual checks for listening. Andrew Watson summarizes a study led by Janet Metcalfe comparing explicit re-teaching to error-focused review for eighth-graders preparing for a high-stakes math exam, finding that interactive, error-focused review outperformed direct instruction during review sessions. Dylan Kane argues that small-group intervention time is usually spent re-teaching content students have already covered, and proposes instead using it to pre-teach upcoming content so students arrive at the whole-class lesson already primed to succeed. Barton frames all three as evidence that precise diagnosis of when and why to deploy a technique matters more than the technique itself.
points: Raichura's framework separates three whole-class techniques (I Say You Say, choral response, checks for listening) along three axes -- participation, accountability, and pace -- and argues they should be blended rather than used interchangeably.

The Metcalfe et al. study Watson summarizes found that a teacher's success in error-focused review depended not on how much time she spent on mistakes but on whether her interactions were discussion-based rather than lecture-based.
Kane's reframe of intervention time -- using it to pre-teach upcoming content rather than re-teach past content -- inverts the default assumption behind most small-group pull-out sessions.
Barton's synthesis across all three: surface-level technique choice matters less than the underlying diagnostic judgment about when a technique is warranted.
